source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not keep updating beliefs as evidence arrives. In a 5-round flight-recommendation task that infers a user's hidden preferences, most models improve little after round 1.
numbers: Setup: 5 rounds, 624 simulated users, models Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Figure 2 shows final-round accuracy for LLMs roughly 37-58% (random about 37%), Bayesian Assistant about 81%. Humans (48 simulated users) improved round 1 to 5 (p=0.002) but also fell short of the Bayesian Assistant.
quote: most of the models show little improvement after the first round of interaction
limits: Preference-inference task, not event forecasting. Per-model numbers read from a figure, so approximate.
agent_relevance: S5 revise: a plain LLM tends to lock in its first read and plateau. Revision cannot be trusted to happen just because new evidence is in the context.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Prompt scaffolds did not fix the stalled updating. Chain-of-thought, numeric flight encodings, 30 rounds instead of 5, and base (non-instruct) models all failed to give meaningful improvement.
numbers: Appendix C.1 / Fig 9: CoT prompting, non-interactive prompting with always-correct examples, verbalised LLM posterior, 30-round runs, pre-trained-only models: none gave meaningful gain.
limits: One task family; prompting variants limited to those tried.
agent_relevance: Telling the agent to think step by step in S5 is not enough. Revision needs a structural check, such as an explicit prior, an explicit likelihood ratio and a numeric posterior kept outside the model.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning to copy a Bayesian model's guesses (Bayesian teaching) beat fine-tuning on the right answers (oracle teaching), made models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time, and transferred to unseen domains (hotel, web shopping) and to real human users.
numbers: Bayesian-tuned LLM agreement with Bayesian Assistant about 80%, significantly above original and oracle-tuned. Medium models after tuning beat larger models and the 48-user human sample. Transfer tested on hotel recommendation, web shopping, and 10 human users x 50 option lists.
limits: Needs weight training, which our scaffold does not use.
agent_relevance: Shows the skill is learnable and that holding graded uncertainty beats copying the true label. For us this argues for a scaffold that stores a numeric belief and updates it by rule.

source: Gupta et al. (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian
finding: In a clean biased-coin task with a known posterior, LLMs broadly follow Bayesian updates as in-context examples accumulate. The errors come mostly from badly calibrated priors, not from wrong update steps.
numbers: Models: Gemma-2 2B, Phi-2, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1 8B (base and Instruct), Mistral 7B (base and Instruct), OLMoE, Pythia suite. Trajectory test: 50 flips at p=0.75 then 50 at p=0.25. Parameter count had negligible effect on order dynamics; the 12B Pythia looked worse than smaller ones on total variation distance.
limits: Toy Bernoulli task, small open models, token-probability readout, not verbalised forecasts. The authors say they do not claim LLMs are explicitly Bayesian.
agent_relevance: Updates are not the weak point in simple cases; the starting prior is. So S5 should take a prior from an outside source (base rate) and not rely on the model's own opening guess.

source: Gupta et al. (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian
finding: Telling the model the coin's bias in words had less pull than the flips it saw. Evidence in the context beat instructions.
numbers: Finding (2) in the abstract; bias statement tested at several theta values including 0.20 on the Pythia suite.
quote: in-context evidence outweighs explicit bias instructions
limits: Coin flips only.
agent_relevance: Facts shown in context will override a stated prior in the prompt. Put the prior as a number next to the evidence, not as a prose instruction.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: A large preregistered test of 38 prompts found that an explicit Bayesian-reasoning prompt (start with a prior, update on each piece of information) made forecasts significantly worse across all models.
numbers: Study 1: 37 treatment prompts vs 1 control, 4 models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B), 100 questions, about 3,636-3,771 usable forecasts per model. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction only Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select differed from control, both worse. Bayesian Reasoning, Propose-Evaluate-Select and CoT made forecasts more extreme (17.2-19.9 points from 50%) than control (about 11.9-13.4).
quote: consistently decreased forecasting accuracy across all models
limits: One-shot prompt, no real multi-step updating. Authors suspect shallow mimicry of Bayesian form. Brier gaps are small in absolute size.
agent_relevance: Do not add a prompt that just says 'be Bayesian'. If S5 uses priors and posteriors it must be with checked arithmetic and a pull toward base rates.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Base-rate prompts gave small gains. Base Rate First, Frequency-Based Reasoning and Step-Back beat control after correction in the mixed-effects analysis, though the preregistered primary analysis found no positive prompt effects.
numbers: Study 2 added compound prompts and outside prompts, plus reasoning models o1 and o1-mini. Base Rate First prompt: use the historical frequency of similar events as a starting point, then adjust. Combined Base Rate + Frequency prompt gave mean forecast 38.4% (SD 0.235) vs control mean 50%.
quote: references to base rates yield slight benefits
limits: Effects are slight. The paper concludes prompt engineering alone is unlikely to do much for forecasting.
agent_relevance: Anchor on an outside-view base rate, then adjust, is the one revision-shaped prompt that helped. It fits S5 as 'start from the base rate, then move'.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 2: when GPT-4 and Claude 2 were shown the human crowd median and asked to update, their Brier scores improved and their intervals narrowed, and they moved in proportion to the gap.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003). Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001). Interval width GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22, Claude 2 11.67 to 8.28 (both p<0.001). Correlation between initial gap and size of revision: r=0.88 (GPT-4), r=0.87 (Claude 2). Questions from a Metaculus tournament, Oct 2023-Jan 2024.
limits: Two models, median handed to them. The paper also compared the updated forecast with a simple machine-human average as an exploratory check; that result was not extracted here.
agent_relevance: LLMs revise sensibly and in proportion when given a strong external signal. A scaffold step that injects a reference class or crowd figure and asks for an update is supported.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 1: a crowd of 12 LLMs matched the human crowd on accuracy. Models showed acquiescence bias, forecasting above 50% on a question set where fewer than half resolved yes.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd M=0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850 (no significant difference). Median forecast across all models 60%; crowd mean forecast 57.35 (SD 20.93). 925 human forecasters in the tournament.
limits: Equivalence test was not preregistered. Models gave ranges, and midpoints were used.
agent_relevance: Our agent's raw estimates will lean yes. Revision needs a check for direction bias.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval plus reasoning plus ensembling system came near the human crowd but did not match it. It did better when the crowd was unsure and early in a question's life, and worse as more evidence arrived late.
numbers: Test set from 1 June 2023 or later, 5 retrieval dates per question (geometric schedule). System Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. When crowd was between 0.3 and 0.7: system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. Better at retrieval dates 1-3, not 4-5. Best base model alone (GPT-4-1106-Preview) Brier 0.208; 50% baseline 0.25.
quote: the system nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters
limits: Retrieval dates simulate a past 'now'. The late-evidence gap may reflect weak use of late news, hedging, or both.
agent_relevance: Crowd forecasters gain more from later evidence than the machine does. That is a measure of weak updating on new information and a target for S5.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The model hedges. It rarely outputs very low or very high probabilities, so it loses on questions where the crowd is nearly certain even though it is more often right.
numbers: On questions where the crowd forecast is within 0.05 of 0 or 1, system accuracy is 7% higher but Brier is 0.04 worse. Authors blame safety training pulling toward the middle.
limits: Hypothesis, supported by a qualitative example.
agent_relevance: Small steps are good; steps that never travel are not. S5 must let a well-supported belief move toward the extremes.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Self-supervised fine-tuning on the model's own best reasonings, filtered to beat the crowd, improved forecasting. Ensembling by trimmed mean worked best of five methods.
numbers: 73,632 reasonings generated; 13,253 kept as fine-tuning data (lower Brier than crowd; pairs deviating strongly dropped to limit overconfidence). Final ensemble: trimmed mean over base and fine-tuned forecasts.
limits: Uses weights; questions come from platforms with a known crowd.
agent_relevance: Aggregating several independent revisions and trimming outliers is a usable S5 control that has been shown to help.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: How consistently a model's forecasts hold together across related questions tracks its real forecasting skill. One check is built on expected evidence: a forecast should equal the mix of the conditional forecasts.
numbers: Ten checks: Negation, Paraphrase, Consequence, AndOr, And, Or, But, Cond, CondCond, ExpEvidence. Aggregated correlation with Brier scores ranged 0.49-0.85 depending on metric and question set. Cond correlations 0.92, 0.87, 0.71, 0.69; CondCond 0.78, 0.71, 0.75, 0.69. ExpEvidence: 0.20, 0.77, -0.11, 0.06 across the four metric and set combinations.
limits: Correlation across a handful of forecasters. ExpEvidence, the check closest to belief updating, was unstable across question sets. Even reasoning models (o1-mini) were inconsistent.
agent_relevance: The check F(P)=F(P|Q)F(Q)+F(P|not Q)(1-F(Q)) can run inside an agent as a coherence test on a revision. The conditional-probability checks carry the most signal.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: A forecaster wrapper that fixes its own inconsistencies (ArbitrageForecaster) lowers violations on negation and paraphrase checks.
numbers: Tested with gpt-4o-mini base and recursive wrappers (Appendix F). A consistency benchmark that resolves in 2028 is released.
limits: Few setups tested; recursive runs are costly; not consistent on every check by construction.
agent_relevance: A cheap self-consistency loop (ask, ask the negation, reconcile) is a candidate for the schema's revise state.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning
finding: On Belief-R, a test of whether a model drops a prior conclusion when a new premise undercuts it, strong models could infer but barely revised. They trade updating against keeping a belief.
numbers: 30 LMs, three prompts (direct, CoT, plan-and-solve). Models above 6B scored over 75% on basic inference (instruct models over 90%). Yet most non-API models were near 0% on Belief Update accuracy. Best models reached at most about 50% on BREU (mean of update and maintain accuracy). Llama-3 70B Instruct, direct prompt: update 10.99%, maintain 92.09%, BREU 51.54%.
quote: LMs generally struggle to appropriately revise their beliefs in response to new information
limits: Logical defeasible inference (modus ponens and tollens), not forecasting. Table columns were hard to read from the PDF, so only cells I could read are quoted.
agent_relevance: Models either stick (high maintain, low update) or flip. Both errors need a test. Score S5 on cases where revision is required and on cases where it is not.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning
finding: Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve prompting did not help belief revision. Plan-and-solve added only about 1 point of BREU. Revision was worse for modus tollens and for abstract mental-state effects.
numbers: CoT showed no significant gain (Fig 5c). Models leaned toward keeping beliefs for mental-state effects instead of updating.
limits: Zero-shot prompts only.
agent_relevance: Matches Qiu et al. on CoT. Supports building explicit 'what would change my mind' checks instead of extra reasoning text.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Under social pressure the opposite failure appears: assistants change correct answers when the user says 'are you sure?', with no new evidence. This is updating on the wrong signal.
numbers: Five AI assistants; QA from MMLU, MATH, AQuA, TruthfulQA, TriviaQA. Claude 1.3 wrongly admitted a mistake on 98% of questions it had answered correctly. The effect held even when the model had stated high confidence first.
quote: wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions
limits: Challenge was bare pushback. Human preference data link it to training on human feedback.
agent_relevance: A good S5 must tell new evidence from pressure. Revision should require a stated reason and a named piece of new evidence.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: LLMs are pulled toward the first number they see. Four mitigation prompts did not remove the anchoring effect.
numbers: Dataset from a human anchoring study (Yasseri); GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Chain of Thought, Principle of Thought, Ignore-the-hint and Reflection strategies all left the anchor effect with very small p-values. A Both-Anchor strategy (a high and a low hint) brought GPT-4 close to the bias-free value on 8 of 15 questions, those where the hints bracketed it.
limits: Small question set; preprint by school-level authors.
agent_relevance: Order and framing of evidence matter. Supply opposing anchors or several reference classes together instead of asking the model to ignore one.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: A 13,465-prompt test of anchoring, primacy, framing, status-quo and group bias in LLMs found mitigation works only partly. Awareness prompts help some models; few-shot examples sometimes backfire; letting the model rewrite its own prompt (self-help) is the main method the authors propose.
numbers: Llama models changed 40-52% of decisions in the anchoring sequence when allowed to change. Awareness mitigation helped anchoring for Llama; few-shot led to failure cases.
limits: Admissions-style decisions, not forecasts.
agent_relevance: Generating a debiased restatement as its own step is a cheap method that has been tested and could serve S5.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models
finding: Seven LLMs show irrationality on classic cognitive-psychology tasks, but not in the same way as humans, and their answers vary a lot between runs.
numbers: Tasks include the conjunction fallacy; each response is coded correct or not and human-like or not. Seven models.
limits: Prompt-level tests; numeric rates not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that human-bias fixes transfer. Measure the agent's own revision errors.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Schoenegger (2025) LLMs Can Teach Themselves to Better Predict the Future
finding: Fine-tuning on pairs of the model's own reasonings, ranked by closeness to the real outcome, improved forecasts on resolved Polymarket questions beyond a randomised-label control.
numbers: Phi-4 14B Brier 0.221 base, 0.214 randomised-label control, 0.200 fine-tuned. DeepSeek-R1 14B 0.211 base, 0.212 control, 0.197 fine-tuned. N=2,300 questions.
limits: Weights change; effect sizes in Brier are about 0.01-0.02.
agent_relevance: Outcome-ranked self-play shows revision quality can be improved from resolutions alone. A log of our agent's forecast and outcome pairs could guide offline schema tuning.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: RL with a Brier reward on a 14B model reached about the level of o1 with better calibration. Per-question standard-deviation scaling was removed because it can encourage overconfidence.
numbers: 1,265 hold-out Polymarket questions; seven-run ReMax ensemble Brier 0.190 [0.178, 0.203], ECE 0.062; no model beat the Polymarket price alone.
limits: Distilled Qwen 14B; weights trained.
agent_relevance: Reward design matters: the loss shapes how boldly a model updates. Our scaffold should score revisions with a proper scoring rule.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: On the 200-question human set, superforecasters beat the best LLM and the public. LLMs were much worse on combination questions.
numbers: Superforecasters Brier 0.096; public 0.121; best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122, p<0.001 vs superforecasters. LLM set: 1,000 questions (500 standard, 500 combination). Public sample: 500 recruited via Prolific and Facebook.
limits: Early-2025 models; the leaderboard is live and changes.
agent_relevance: Combination questions need probabilities that stay coherent when separate revisions are combined. Test this in the agent.

source: Wildman et al. (2025) Bench to the Future: A Pastcasting Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
finding: A pastcasting benchmark (a frozen web snapshot per question) lets agents be scored on evidence gathering and updating without waiting for outcomes. Agents with evidence beat no-evidence LLMs, though no-evidence models still beat the 0.25 coin-flip Brier.
numbers: 299 binary questions (87 original, 135 from multiple-choice, 77 from numeric), effective N about 178.8. ReAct agent, fixed- and variable-evidence forecasters and a no-evidence baseline across Claude 3.5/3.7/4 and Gemini 2.5 Pro. 20 live-vs-retro questions used to check validity.
limits: Contamination risk grows as model cutoffs advance. Most pairwise model differences were not significant.
agent_relevance: A ReAct loop of thought, search, observation is the agent form of updating on evidence. Pastcasting is a way to test our S5 offline.

source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang, Ma (2022) An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
finding: Theory with small synthetic tests that in-context learning can be seen as implicit Bayesian inference over a latent concept. Background for why in-context belief updating can look Bayesian.
numbers: not read in detail this session; PDF header only
limits: Synthetic pretraining setup.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that updates happen in context, with priors set by pretraining.

source: Atanasov, Witkowski, Mellers, Tetlock (2020) Small Steps to Accuracy: Incremental Belief Updaters Are Better Forecasters
finding: Human baseline for this subfield: forecasters who update often in small steps scored better than those who update rarely or in big jumps in the Good Judgment tournaments. Not opened this session; listed for reference to the human-side files.
numbers: not verified this session
limits: Cited from memory; the human data are covered by other agents on this subfield.
agent_relevance: This is the human target that the LLM studies above fall short of: frequent small moves in proportion to the evidence.

source: Tetlock and Gardner (2015) Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
finding: Source of the advice to update in small steps and neither under- nor over-react, from the Good Judgment Project.
numbers: not verified this session
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Human origin of the S5 rule.
